title: Yacht Rock
kicker: 60 crossings in smooth water · 1972 to 1983, mostly out of LA
description: A walk through 60 smooth, session-player soft rock songs from 1972 to 1983, with a taste of each, what to listen for, and how the same few musicians tie them together.
lede: For about seven years the same few dozen Los Angeles session players turned up on half the soft-rock radio: a Porcaro on drums, a Rhodes under the verse, Michael McDonald somewhere in the backing vocals. Nobody called it yacht rock until a web series did in 2005. This is that run, one song at a time, in the order the records came out, with a few that came before and one that came after.

eras.name: Canyon Morning
eras.essay: In 1972 this music had no name and no home town. Seals & Crofts cut 'Summer Breeze' at the Sound Factory in Hollywood. Looking Glass made 'Brandy' at Regent Sound in New York after a false start with Steve Cropper in Memphis, and a Washington DJ turned the B-side into a number one. Ace were English and recorded 'How Long' at Rockfield in Wales. Meanwhile the country had a rough few years. The oil embargo of October 1973 took a barrel from about $3 to nearly $12, Nixon resigned on 9 August 1974, and Saigon fell in April 1975. By 1976 the money and the players had settled in Los Angeles. Boz Scaggs hired David Paich, Jeff Porcaro and David Hungate for Silk Degrees, which spent 115 weeks on the Billboard 200 and sent all three off to form Toto. Steely Dan had stopped touring, so their touring keyboard player Michael McDonald was free when Tom Johnston's ulcers took him off the road, and the Doobie Brothers cut Takin' It to the Streets at Warner Bros. in North Hollywood. Steely Dan started The Royal Scam at Davlen in North Hollywood, decamped to New York, and finished at ABC in LA. The name came 29 years later, from a 2005 online comedy series called Yacht Rock.

eras.name: Rhodes After Dark
eras.essay: Disco owned the album chart for most of this stretch. The Saturday Night Fever soundtrack sat at No. 1 for 24 straight weeks from January 1978, and the record that finally knocked it off, on 8 July, was Gerry Rafferty's City to City, cut in a studio in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire. ABC had launched The Love Boat the previous September, so soft rock had its ship before it had its name. The LA rooms were busy. The Doobies made Minute by Minute at Warner Bros. Studios in North Hollywood, Toto spent nine months between Studio 55, Davlen and Sunset Sound, and Ambrosia worked at Mama Jo's. A lot of this era was made somewhere else, though. Peg was the one Aja track recorded in New York, and Carly Simon's Boys in the Trees and Kenny Loggins's Nightwatch were New York records too. Bobby Caldwell cut his debut at TK in Hialeah, Florida, Paul Davis worked in Atlanta for Bang, and Little River Band were at Armstrong Studios in South Melbourne. By now the sound travelled: a Rhodes, a session drummer who played behind the beat, and a singer who sounded hurt but well rested. Aja was one of the first albums to go Platinum, a certification the RIAA had only just started handing out.

scene.artifact: The Love Boat: ABC put the series on air on 24 September 1977, set it on Princess Cruises' real Pacific Princess, had Jack Jones sing the theme, and kept it sailing for 250 episodes until 1986.

eras.name: Record of the Year
eras.essay: 1979 was a rough year to sell records and a good one to sell this kind. Disco blew up in public on 12 July, when a Chicago shock jock detonated a crate of disco LPs between games of a White Sox doubleheader at Comiskey Park and the crowd tore up the field. The gas lines were back, crude went from $15.85 a barrel in April to $39.50 a year later, and on 15 July Jimmy Carter went on television to talk about a crisis of confidence. Soft rock with a soul engine under it filled the gap. What a Fool Believes, written by Michael McDonald and Kenny Loggins, topped the Hot 100 on 14 April and took Record of the Year the next February, and McDonald turns up twice more in this era, as Loggins's harmony and as the answering voice on Ride Like the Wind. Warner Bros. signed Christopher Cross out of Austin early in the year, and Michael Omartian cut his debut on 3M's digital recorder, one of the first pop albums made that way. David Foster and Jay Graydon handed a ballad to Earth, Wind & Fire. The Eagles took eighteen months over The Long Run and split the year after. Rupert Holmes closed the decade at number one with a song about a personals ad.

gear: 3M 79 24-track with a custom API console at Amigo Studios
scene.artifact: The 22nd Grammy Awards at the Shrine Auditorium on 27 February 1980: What a Fool Believes won Record and Song of the Year over After the Love Has Gone, and Rickie Lee Jones beat the Knack, Dire Straits, the Blues Brothers and Robin Williams to Best New Artist.

eras.name: Satin Wake
eras.essay: Gaucho cost a dollar more than other records. In late 1980 MCA made it a test case for 'superstar pricing' at $9.98, and Steely Dan worried their fans would blame them. Becker and Fagen had used at least 42 session players over more than a year, and handed engineer Roger Nichols $150,000 of the budget to build Wendel, a drum machine that played the beat they wanted. Quincy Jones started Qwest Records with Warner Bros. in 1980, opened it with George Benson's Give Me the Night and signed his goddaughter Patti Austin. Jay Graydon spent 1981 producing Al Jarreau and writing a Benson single with Steve Lukather and Bill Champlin. At the February 1981 Grammys Robbie Dupree, whose hit sounded a lot like the Doobies, lost Best New Artist to Christopher Cross, who won all four general awards that night. By October Cross was at number one again with the theme to Arthur, a $7 million Dudley Moore comedy that made $95.5 million. The machines came in on both coasts. The Linn LM-1 went on sale in 1980 at $5,500, with no cymbal sounds, and Jeff Porcaro programmed one for Benson. In New York, Daryl Hall built a number one on a Roland preset called Rock 1. MTV switched on at 12:01 a.m. on 1 August 1981.

gear: Wendel, Roger Nichols' custom drum machine
scene.artifact: Wendel, the drum machine Roger Nichols built for Steely Dan with $150,000 of the Gaucho budget, which got its own RIAA platinum record when the album sold a million.

eras.name: Last Light on the Water
eras.essay: By 1982 the session players who had spent six years making other people's records sound expensive were cashing in under their own names. Toto made Toto IV at Sunset Sound and Record One between June 1981 and January 1982, and on 23 February 1983, at the Shrine Auditorium, the band went home with six Grammys, Record and Album of the Year among them. The same people were across town at Westlake, where Quincy Jones spent April to November 1982 making Thriller on a $750,000 budget. Chicago left Columbia for Warner and handed David Foster the controls. The money was moving to pictures. MTV went on air at 12:01 a.m. on 1 August 1981, and Steve Barron shot the videos for 'Rosanna', 'Africa' and 'Billie Jean'. MTV only put 'Billie Jean' into rotation on 10 March 1983, after CBS Records boss Walter Yetnikoff threatened to pull every CBS video off the channel. The sound was moving as well. Donald Fagen cut The Nightfly on 3M digital recorders, the first CDs went on sale in Japan on 1 October 1982, and in 1983 Yamaha's $1,995 DX7 arrived with an electric piano preset that led some players to drop the Rhodes for it. By 'Yah Mo B There' the drums are a LinnDrum and the keyboards are a stack of synthesizers.

scene.artifact: Steve Barron's video for 'Rosanna': a West Side Story street set, Cynthia Rhodes in a red dress, an uncredited Patrick Swayze among the dancers, and Mike Porcaro miming bass parts David Hungate had played, the session band's look as MTV wanted it.
